title: Ang Thong Craft Trip: Drum & Doll Villages, 2 Days | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A 2-day craft itinerary in Ang Thong, Thailand. Watch artisans stretch drum skins at Ban Ekkarat drum village in Pa Mok, then see clay court-dolls made at Ban Bang Sadet, plus timing, route, and the giant reclining Buddha at Wat Pa Mok.
keywords: Ang Thong travel, Ban Ekkarat drum village, Bang Sadet court dolls, Pa Mok Ang Thong, Ang Thong 2-day itinerary
h1:
Ang Thong Craft Trail
Ban Ekkarat Drums & Ban Bang Sadet Dolls
intro: Ang Thong is a small province where folk craft is still a living, working trade, not just something behind museum glass. Pa Mok district has two villages where people still make things by hand every day: Ban Ekkarat drum village, where they stretch cowhide over drum bodies right out front, and the Ban Bang Sadet court-doll centre, where locals shape clay into little dolls that tell Thai everyday life. We've laid this out as an easy two-day, drive-yourself plan that lets you watch real artisans at both spots, with a stop at Wat Pa Mok to see the giant reclining Buddha along the way.

blocks.html: Both villages sit in Pa Mok district, only a few kilometres apart. From Ang Thong town, take Highway 309 (the Ang Thong–Ayutthaya road) and you'll reach the Pa Mok area in about 15–18 km. It suits travellers who want to slow down, chat with the makers and watch the steps of the work rather than snap a photo and move on. Coming from Bangkok, it's roughly an hour and a half by car. You can do it as a single early-start day trip, but staying one night lets you add the temples and the Chao Phraya riverside without rushing.

blocks.text: Why Pa Mok — craft that's still alive

blocks.html: The drum village in Ekkarat sub-district has been making drums for sale since around 1927. It started with locals being hired to stretch the skins on temple bass drums nearby, then grew into a full trade. Today about 20 households make drums and sell them out front, with another dozen or so supplying shops. The drums are turned from soft chamcha (rain tree) wood for the body, then covered with cowhide and pinned tack by tack — work that comes down purely to the hands and the ear.

The Bang Sadet court dolls, meanwhile, are a SUPPORT Arts and Crafts (Silpacheep) project that Her Majesty Queen Sirikit started back in 1976, giving villagers who had good clay (once used for bricks) a side income and helping revive a court-doll craft that had nearly died out. The dolls are shaped from clay and tell Thai life — children's games, Thai music ensembles, processions, even Thai fruit — making them souvenirs with a story built in.

blocks.title: When you'll actually see the artisans at work
blocks.html: At both spots the handwork is busiest from morning until early afternoon. If you want to see the real process and not just a shop counter, go before noon. The court-doll centre opens daily 08:00–16:00. The drum village is a cluster of artisans' homes that open house by house — just stop and chat, but avoid the lunch break.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Ban Ekkarat drum village + Wat Pa Mok

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Pa Mok: drums and the reclining Buddha

items.activity: Leave Ang Thong town / arrive in Pa Mok
items.note: From town it's about 15–18 km on Highway 309. There are petrol stations and roadside coffee shops to fuel up before you reach the village.

items.activity: Walk Ban Ekkarat drum village (behind Pa Mok market)
items.note: Watch artisans turn the chamcha wood, stretch the cowhide and drive in the tacks one by one. The homes line up next to each other, so you can stroll past several and talk to the owners directly.

items.activity: Pick up a drum as a souvenir
items.note: Sizes run from small ramwong dance drums and long klong yao drums up to big temple bass drums. Small ones travel home with you; for big ones, the shops can arrange delivery. Tap and listen to the tone before you choose.
Pa Mok is a riverside community with noodle shops and local rice-and-curry spots at local prices.

items.activity: Wat Pa Mok Worawihan, pay respects to the reclining Buddha
items.note: A lacquered, gilded stucco reclining Buddha about 22.58 m long — one of Thailand's beautiful old reclining images. The temple sits by the Chao Phraya, a pleasant spot for an evening stroll.

items.activity: Walk along the Chao Phraya on the Pa Mok side
items.note: Take photos, sip a coffee and watch riverside life before heading back to your room in Ang Thong town.

blocks.html: A small tip at the drum village: ask the makers which wood a given drum is made from and how many layers of skin it has, because the price changes with the size and the handwork. The artisans here are happy to explain, and some houses will even let you try driving a tack or giving the drum a hit. If you're travelling with kids, this part is more fun than you'd expect.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Ban Bang Sadet court-doll centre

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Ban Bang Sadet: handmade clay dolls

items.activity: Leave your room for Ban Bang Sadet
items.note: Also in Pa Mok district, near Wat Tha Sutthawat. It's about 20 km from town, and the signs are clear.

items.activity: Enter the Ban Bang Sadet court-doll centre
items.note: The centre is a large wooden Thai-style house in the grounds of Wat Tha Sutthawat, open daily 08:00–16:00. You can go in and watch locals actually shaping the dolls.

items.activity: Watch the shaping and painting of the court dolls
items.note: From forming the clay and drying it to painting and adding the fine detail. The sets you'll see most often are Thai children's games, the pi phat ensemble, processions, and the Thai fruit set.

items.activity: Buy a doll as a souvenir / try shaping one yourself
items.note: It's a royal Silpacheep craft, so buying directly supports the community. At some times visitors can try shaping a doll, which is great for families.
The temple is right next to the centre, with murals and a riverside setting you can walk through without driving anywhere.

items.activity: Add Wat Muang's giant Buddha (if you have the energy)
items.note: Ang Thong's huge Buddha image, in a different district, about 30–40 min more by car — a good highlight to close the trip.

items.name: Small ramwong / klong yao drum
items.blurb: From Ban Ekkarat, hand-sized and easy to carry home. Tap and listen to the tone before you buy; small ones are affordable.

items.name: Court-doll set of Thai games
items.blurb: Hand-shaped at Ban Bang Sadet, featuring kids playing mon son pha and ri ri khao san — charming and full of story.

items.name: Thai fruit doll set
items.blurb: Clay shaped into tiny Thai fruits, lovely on a shelf and a souvenir you won't easily find elsewhere.

blocks.html: Both crafts are made by hand, one piece at a time, so they don't cost what factory goods do — but that's exactly why they're worth it. Buying straight from the makers keeps this knowledge breathing, especially the court dolls, which struggled badly during the COVID years.

items: Your own vehicle is easiest — the two villages and the temples are spread across Pa Mok district and public transport barely reaches them, so driving yourself or renting a car/motorbike is far smoother.
From Bangkok — about 1.5 hours by car, past Ayutthaya onto Highway 309, reaching Pa Mok before you get to Ang Thong town.
Go in the morning to see the work clearly — the handwork is busy from morning to early afternoon; avoid late afternoon, when many houses close or take a break.
Bring cash — many artisans' shops mainly take cash; some do accept QR payment, but not all.
Big drums can be shipped — if you fall for a large temple drum or long drum, talk to the shop about delivery so you don't have to haul it yourself.

blocks.title: Pairing the trip to make it worthwhile
blocks.html: If you only have one day, do the drum village in the morning plus Wat Pa Mok in the afternoon — that fills a day nicely — and save Ban Bang Sadet for next time. But if you stay overnight, you get both villages unhurried plus Wat Muang's giant Buddha to finish.

faq.q: Are Ban Ekkarat drum village and Ban Bang Sadet far apart?
faq.a: Both are in Pa Mok district, only a few kilometres apart and a few minutes' drive from each other. From Ang Thong town it's about 15–20 km along Highway 309. You can easily visit both on the same trip.

faq.q: What are the Ban Bang Sadet court-doll centre's hours, and is there an entry fee?
faq.a: It's open daily 08:00–16:00 in the grounds of Wat Tha Sutthawat. You can watch the shaping and buy dolls as souvenirs. Go from morning to early afternoon to catch the locals actually at work.

faq.q: Can you really watch artisans at the drum village, or is it just shops?
faq.a: You really can. It's a cluster of about 20 artisan households, and many make drums right out front — turning the wood, stretching the cowhide, driving the tacks. You can talk to the makers directly, and some houses let you try hitting or tacking a drum. Go before noon to see the process most clearly.

faq.q: Is one day enough for this itinerary?
faq.a: If you push a bit, a single day works: the drum village in the morning, then Wat Pa Mok, then Ban Bang Sadet in the afternoon. But if you want to take it slow, chat with the makers and add Wat Muang's giant Buddha, one night in Ang Thong town fits better.

faq.q: How do you take a big drum home?
faq.a: Small drums like ramwong dance drums travel home with you. For long drums or big temple bass drums, most artisan shops can arrange delivery — sort out the shipping cost with the shop first, and tap and listen to the tone you like before buying.
